clue.text: Rome rising to create the Italian Renaissance

definitions.text: Rome rising to create the Italian Renaissance

parts.words: Rome rising to create the Italian Renaissance
parts.note: the Italian word for the nineteenth-century national revival literally means a rising again, and Rome became the capital of the new united kingdom

explanation.surface: A history lesson about the city of Rome bringing about the artistic rebirth of Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Italian Renaissance' here is not the fifteenth-century flowering of art but the nineteenth-century movement that unified Italy, whose name means resurgence.
explanation.definitionFit: The movement for Italian unification is named by a word meaning resurgence, a political rebirth of the nation.

clue.text: Pedestrian rose

explanation.definitionFit: A walker who strolls for pleasure is one sense; a climbing variety of garden rose bush is the other.

clue.text: It's Sparta's turn for governors

indicators.note: the clue's own word is turned round, so the letters of the city's possessive are read from the end

explanation.surface: Sparta's turn has come to supply provincial governors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' reverses the letters of SPARTA'S, apostrophe dropped, to give SATRAPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Satraps were the provincial governors of ancient Persia; the word now means any subordinate ruler.

clue.text: It requires a ruler, naturally, to provide this

definitions.text: It requires a ruler, naturally, to provide this

parts.words: It requires a ruler, naturally, to provide this
parts.note: a ruler suggests a measuring stick for drawing a straight mark, but here it is a monarch, whose descendants continue the dynasty

explanation.surface: A geometry hint: you naturally need a ruler to draw this.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the ruler you draw lines with; the 'ruler' is a king or queen, and 'naturally' points to children by birth carrying on the succession.
explanation.definitionFit: A succession of monarchs descended from one sovereign forms the dynasty's line of heirs.

clue.text: Conclude that it's hell without a negative

indicators.note: without tells us to take the negative word away from the word for hell

parts.note: the Inferno is hell, as in Dante
no is a negative reply

explanation.surface: Someone decides that hell would be a place with no negatives at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes NO from INFERNO.
explanation.definitionFit: To deduce or reason out a conclusion from evidence is the meaning of the answer.

clue.text: Make quick erratic line to the archdeacon

indicators.note: erratic means wandering irregularly, so the letters of line are scrambled

parts.note: Ven, short for Venerable, is the title of an archdeacon

explanation.surface: A cleric tries to speed up a wandering queue at his door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'erratic' rearranges LINE into ENLI; an archdeacon is styled the Venerable, abbreviated VEN. 'quick' is in the old sense 'alive'.
explanation.definitionFit: Quick in its old sense means alive, as in 'the quick and the dead', so to animate or bring life to something.

clue.text: They follow established lines

parts.note: people or devices that copy over an existing drawing go along lines already laid down

explanation.surface: Conformists who stick to the accepted way of doing things.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests conservative people keeping to tradition; literally these are things that go over lines already drawn, as tracing paper or a tracer bullet's path does.
explanation.definitionFit: A person or tool that copies a drawing by going over its lines, or anything that marks out a path.

clue.text: Commuters who, in the rush hour …

definitions.text: Commuters who, in the rush hour …

parts.words: Commuters who, in the rush hour
parts.note: passengers on a crowded train hold an overhead loop when no seat is free; the clue runs on into the next one

explanation.surface: A description of rush-hour commuters, continued in the clue that follows.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this clue to 10 Down: commuters in the rush hour can only have standing room, so they hold the hanging straps.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing passengers who grip the loops hung from the roof of a bus or train carriage.

clue.text: Name for a grass-widower ?

parts.note: a grass-widower is a man whose wife is away, but read literally he would be a man married to a grass, and this man's name is also a kind of meadow grass

explanation.surface: Suggesting a suitable name for a husband whose wife is away.
explanation.walkthrough: A grass-widower is a man temporarily apart from his wife; the clue pretends his wife was a grass, so he takes the name of a pasture grass that is also a man's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A male first name that is also a common hay and pasture grass, Phleum pratense.

clue.text: Sound chaps, the Egyptian peasants

indicators.note: Sound signals that the word is heard rather than spelt, so the answer only sounds like a slang word

parts.note: fellas is informal for chaps or men

explanation.surface: A remark that the Egyptian peasants are good, sound chaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like praise of the chaps but signals a homophone: FELLAS said out loud gives FELLAHS.
explanation.definitionFit: Fellahin are the agricultural labourers and peasant farmers of Egypt and other Arab countries.

clue.text: … only have this space

parts.note: continuing the previous clue, crowded commuters have space only to stand, the phrase completed by the word only

explanation.surface: The continuation: rush-hour commuters have only this much space.
explanation.walkthrough: Read with 7 Down: the familiar notice 'standing room only' is split so that 'only' follows the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Space in which people may stand because all seats are taken.

clue.text: An entirely chilly greeting

parts.note: all means entirely or wholly
hail is icy precipitation, something chilly

explanation.surface: A thoroughly frosty welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chilly' stands loosely for hail, frozen pellets of rain.
explanation.definitionFit: An old salutation of welcome, as the witches cry to Macbeth.

clue.text: I arrive here in a mess

indicators.note: in a mess says the letters of the words are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A traveller arrives at the resort in a dishevelled state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a mess' rearranges I ARRIVE; the whole clue describes the place where 'I arrive', the resort coast.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Here' points to a destination, the stretch of Mediterranean coast in France and Italy where holidaymakers arrive.

clue.text: Coppers are after her in droves

indicators.note: are after puts the police letters behind the female pronoun in the answer

parts.note: DS stands for detective sergeants, police officers

explanation.surface: Police officers are pursuing a woman in large numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' tempts you towards CU or pennies, but detective sergeants are the police officers wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Droves are large moving crowds of animals or people, as are flocks and herds.

clue.text: Needled, perhaps, but suffering no ill effects

definitions.text: Needled, perhaps, but suffering no ill effects

parts.words: Needled, perhaps, but suffering no ill effects
parts.note: needled seems to mean irritated, but here it is given an injection, which protects against disease

explanation.surface: Someone provoked yet unruffled by the provocation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needled' seems to mean annoyed; it is jabbed with a needle, a vaccination that leaves one safe from infection.
explanation.definitionFit: Vaccinated by injection and so protected against catching a disease.

clue.text: A fly-by-night dances away from them

definitions.text: A fly-by-night dances away from them

parts.words: A fly-by-night dances away from them
parts.note: a night-flying insect keeps clear of the strong-smelling balls laid among clothes; the words also split as the insect plus dances

explanation.surface: A shady character dances away from the people chasing him.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'fly-by-night' is usually a rogue; here it is a moth, and 'dances' are balls, so the clue spells MOTH + BALLS while saying moths keep away from them.
explanation.definitionFit: Small balls of naphthalene stored with clothes keep insects that eat fabric away.

clue.text: He supplies our daily needs

parts.note: daily needs sounds like groceries but means the daily papers delivered by a shopkeeper

explanation.surface: A grocer or provider who keeps us stocked with essentials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'daily needs' suggests food; the needs are dailies, the morning papers.
explanation.definitionFit: A shopkeeper who sells and delivers newspapers and magazines, the dailies.

clue.text: Was Titipu's noble lord only half so spiteful ?

indicators.note: only half keeps the first part of the lord's name and drops the rest

parts.note: Pish-Tush is a noble lord in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado, set in the town of Titipu

explanation.surface: Asking whether a Gilbert and Sullivan nobleman was only half as spiteful.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mikado, by Gilbert and Sullivan, is set in the Japanese town of Titipu, where Pish-Tush is one of the noble lords.
explanation.definitionFit: Waspish means irritable and sharply spiteful, like a stinging insect.

clue.text: Mine hostess's fish

explanation.definitionFit: An old term for a woman who keeps a pub, the landlady or 'mine hostess'; also a herring-like North American fish.

clue.text: Not a planned feature of a passing-out parade

definitions.text: Not a planned feature of a passing-out parade

parts.words: Not a planned feature of a passing-out parade
parts.note: a passing-out parade marks cadets graduating, but passing out also means fainting, which no one plans

explanation.surface: Something unscheduled at a military graduation ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'passing-out parade' is the ceremony when cadets complete training; read literally, a cadet passing out faints on the parade ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A faint, a sudden loss of consciousness.

clue.text: Cause' of widespread affliction when cures go awry.

indicators.note: awry means askew or gone wrong, so the letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: When attempted remedies go wrong they cause widespread suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awry' rearranges CURES GO. The stray apostrophe after 'Cause' is a printing mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A whip, and figuratively a plague or anything that causes great suffering to many.

clue.text: Excursions ' enjoyed by. the fielding side?

explanation.definitionFit: Trips or outings for pleasure; and in cricket, getting batsmen dismissed, the 'outs' a fielding team relishes.

clue.text: A den set in part of London

indicators.note: in here signals the letters of the phrase being rearranged into a new place

explanation.surface: A den located somewhere in London.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of A DEN SET rearrange to give the district of London east of the City, historically the docklands.
explanation.definitionFit: The area of east London beyond the old City walls, traditionally home of Cockneys.

clue.text: That of Gerontius was noted

parts.note: Elgar set Newman's poem about an old man's vision to music, so it was written out in notes

explanation.surface: Gerontius's vision was well known.
explanation.walkthrough: 'noted' seems to mean famous but means set to musical notes: Elgar's oratorio The Dream of Gerontius.
explanation.definitionFit: A vision during sleep, as in Elgar's oratorio about Gerontius's soul.

clue.text: It has an absorbing interest for the penman

definitions.text: It has an absorbing interest for the penman

parts.words: It has an absorbing interest for the penman
parts.note: absorbing suggests fascinating, but the paper actually soaks up ink from a writer

explanation.surface: Something that a writer finds utterly fascinating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'absorbing' sounds like 'engrossing'; it is literal, the paper soaking up wet ink.
explanation.definitionFit: Absorbent paper used to dry ink after writing with a pen.

clue.text: Did this literary club take life too seriously ?

definitions.text: Did this literary club take life too seriously ?

parts.words: Did this literary club take life too seriously
parts.note: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote stories about a club whose members agree to be killed, so they took life in another sense

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a book club was rather too earnest about living.
explanation.walkthrough: Stevenson's 'The Suicide Club' tells of a society of people who wish to die; 'take life' is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: The deliberate taking of one's own life, as members of Stevenson's fictional club agree to do.

clue.text: Florence's magnificent man

parts.note: Florence here is the Italian city, and its fifteenth-century ruler of the Medici family was known as the Magnificent

explanation.surface: A woman named Florence admiring her splendid boyfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Florence' looks like a woman's name; it is the city, ruled by Lorenzo de' Medici, called il Magnifico.
explanation.definitionFit: Lorenzo de' Medici, ruler of Florence, was known as Lorenzo the Magnificent.

clue.text: A fortiori one cannot serve these ships

definitions.text: A fortiori one cannot serve these ships

parts.words: A fortiori one cannot serve these ships
parts.note: since no man can serve two masters, even more so he cannot serve one more than two; the last word reveals them as vessels

explanation.surface: Logic proving that some ships cannot be crewed.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bible says no one can serve two masters, so 'a fortiori' (all the more) one cannot serve more than that; the masters turn out to be masts on sailing ships.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailing ships with a trio of masts, often called by that count of masters.
